examples: It's all along of you that we missed the tide.
The crop failed, and that along of a summer nobody had seen the like of.
She lost the cottage along of a debt her husband never mentioned.
"All along of the drink," he said, "and nothing else."
He's gone off up the lane along of the dog.
Take the little one along of you and mind the gate.
The boys went down to the river along of their uncle.

senses.head: Because of; owing to — the causal sense
body: From Old English gelang, and usually with all. It's all along of you we missed the tide.

senses.head: Along with; in the company of — the accompaniment sense
body: He's gone off along of the others.
examples: It's all along of you that we missed the tide.
The crop failed, and that along of a summer nobody had seen the like of.
She lost the cottage along of a debt her husband never mentioned.
"All along of the drink," he said, "and nothing else."
He's gone off up the lane along of the dog.
Take the little one along of you and mind the gate.
The boys went down to the river along of their uncle.

entries.русский: из-за, по вине — устар. и диал.; во 2-м знач. вместе с, в компании с
entries.register: archaic and dialectal — English regional speech (West Country, Kentish, later Cockney) from the seventeenth century on, carried into older rural American speech and now met almost only in nineteenth-century fiction, in folk song, and in dialogue written to sound old
entries.variants: 'long of and long of are the same phrase with the first syllable worn away, and they are the commoner spellings in American dialect writing. Alonger is a further-worn British form.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — along of you, along of the drink. No gerund (✗ along of missing the tide) and never a finite clause. It also refuses fronting: there is no Along of you, we missed the tide. The phrase sits after the verb, very often after all.
entries.pattern: [clause] all along of [noun phrase] · [clause] along of [noun phrase] · (sense 2) come / go / take [something] along of [pronoun]
entries.contrast: Two senses that look like one word and are not. The causal sense descends from Old English gelang ("dependent on, owing to") and has nothing to do with motion at all; the accompaniment sense is the ordinary along of along with. The two fell together in spelling centuries ago and have been confusing readers of dialect ever since. In the causal sense it is a country cousin of because of and on account of, and like them it belongs to speech. Do not read it as ordinary modern usage — a present-day American who writes all along of the weather is writing costume drama, and the only live reason to know the phrase is that Hardy, Kipling, and the ballads are full of it.
entries.see also: on account of, because of, 'count of, along with, with

entries.meaning: Assigns an effect, or a measured portion of one, to a cause. The object is the cause and the noun in front of the phrase is the effect, which puts it on the same side of the direction trap as as a result of.
examples: Most of the decline is attributable to a single bad quarter.
Roughly a third of the increase is attributable to population growth alone.
Deaths attributable to secondhand smoke have fallen by half since 1990.
The cost overrun is attributable to delays nobody could have foreseen.
Losses attributable to the outage were covered under the policy.
The discrepancy is attributable to having used last year's figures.
Only a small part of the warming is attributable to natural variation.
entries.русский: объясняемый чем-л., относимый на счёт чего-л. — книжн., о доле причины
entries.register: formal — audits, reports, epidemiology, and the courts
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (attributable to having used last year's figures). Never a finite clause — attributable to the fact that is the clause form, and it is clumsy enough that because is nearly always better.
entries.pattern: [noun] is attributable to [noun phrase] · [noun] attributable to [noun phrase] · directly / largely / wholly / partly / in part attributable to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is the phrase the whole due to rule is built on: the traditional test for due to is whether attributable to can be swapped in, and where it can, due to is safe under every analysis — see the due to rule at the end of this file. Like adjectival due to, it follows be or postmodifies a noun and does not front: Attributable to fog, the flight was canceled is not English, where Due to fog, … at least gets argued about. Against because of, it is cooler and more quantitative, and it is the word of choice wherever a share of an effect is being assigned rather than a whole one.
entries.see also: due to, because of, resulting from, as a result of, owing to, consequent on

entries.meaning: Names the cause of whatever the main clause reports. It modifies the verb or the entire clause, and that adverbial job is exactly what the traditional usage rule reserved for it and denied to due to. It is neutral about whether the cause is welcome, which is what separates it from thanks to (grateful or sarcastic), courtesy of (wry), and owing to (formal).
examples: The flight was canceled because of fog.
Because of the strike, deliveries are running two days late.
She missed the deadline because of a family emergency.
He got the job because of who he knows, not what he knows.
Because of being out of the country all spring, he never received the notice.
Attendance is down, mostly because of the parking.
We're only here because of you.
entries.русский: из-за, по причине — основной, нейтральный предлог причины
entries.register: neutral — the default causal preposition of American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (because of being late), or a fused relative, which is still a noun phrase (because of who he knows, because of what she said). Never a finite clause and never a that-clause. The clause form is the conjunction because standing alone — because it rained, never because of it rained and never because of that it rained.
entries.pattern: [clause] because of [noun phrase] · Because of [noun phrase], [clause] · because of [verb-ing] · partly / largely / mainly / only / precisely because of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Because + clause against because of + noun phrase is the cleanest preposition/conjunction pair in the language: We stayed home because it rained / We stayed home because of the rain. Against due to, because of is adverbial by nature and no editor has ever objected to it, which makes it the safe choice whenever you are unsure — see the due to rule at the end of this file. Against owing to and on account of, it is the plain, unmarked word. The internet construction because science, because reasons puts a bare noun after because alone; it is a deliberate joke and is not standard English.
entries.see also: due to, owing to, on account of, as a result of, thanks to, attributable to, because of (complex prepositions), because (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Names the legal machinery itself as the cause: the result follows from a rule, automatically, without an act by any party.
examples: On her death the title passed to the survivor by operation of law.
This lease may not be assigned, whether voluntarily or by operation of law.
The debt was discharged by operation of law when the limitations period ran out.
The easement was extinguished by operation of the merger doctrine, not by any release.
A dissolved corporation loses its franchise by operation of the statute rather than by any act of the secretary of state.
In most states an earlier will was revoked by operation of law on marriage until the probate code was rewritten.
Nothing in this section prevents a transfer by operation of law to a surviving spouse.
entries.русский: в силу (закона) — юр.; о последствии, наступающем автоматически, без чьих-либо действий
entries.register: legal — statutes, deeds, title opinions, and the anti-assignment clause of almost every commercial contract; the one place a non-lawyer meets it is the fixed phrase by operation of law
entries.complement: noun phrase, and in practice a very short list of them — law, the statute, this section, the trust instrument, the merger doctrine. No gerund (✗ by operation of transferring the deed) and never a finite clause. The object names a rule, never a person: ✗ by operation of the trustee.
entries.pattern: by operation of law · [clause] by operation of [statute or instrument] · by operation of law or otherwise · whether by agreement or by operation of law
entries.contrast: Names a consequence that arrives automatically, with nobody acting to bring it about — which is the whole content of the phrase and the reason drafters cannot do without it. A joint tenant's share passes by operation of law the moment the co-tenant dies, and no one signs anything; that is why an anti-assignment clause says by operation of law or otherwise, to catch the transfers a merger or a death produces without an assignment. Against by virtue of, which names the standing or qualification that lets somebody act, and against pursuant to, which names authority somebody is exercising: both of those have a human actor behind them and by operation of deliberately has none.
entries.see also: by virtue of, by reason of, pursuant to, under and pursuant to, in consideration of

entries.meaning: The formal, chiefly legal way of naming a cause or a ground. In modern American writing it appears almost entirely in statutes, insurance policies, and court filings, plus the set phrases those documents have pushed out into general use.
examples: He was found not guilty by reason of insanity.
No applicant may be refused by reason of race, religion, or national origin.
The lease terminates by reason of the tenant's default.
Benefits were denied by reason of his failure to file on time.
She was excused from jury service by reason of ill health.
Any loss by reason of fire is covered under Section 4.
entries.русский: по причине, вследствие — юр. и книжн.; вне канцелярии звучит напыщенно
entries.register: legal and formal — outside statutes and pleadings it sounds stilted
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically an abstract one (by reason of insanity, by reason of age). A gerund is possible (by reason of having served twenty years) but uncommon. Never a finite clause — the clausal form is the archaic by reason that.
entries.pattern: [clause] by reason of [noun phrase] · [noun] by reason of [noun phrase] · not guilty by reason of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Because of means the same thing and is shorter. By reason of survives because legal drafting is conservative and because a handful of fixed phrases have hardened around it — not guilty by reason of insanity, disqualified by reason of age. Do not confuse it with by virtue of, which names a qualification that enables something rather than a cause that produces it: you hold the seat by virtue of your office and you lose it by reason of your conviction.
entries.see also: by virtue of, because of, on the grounds of, on account of, in consequence of

entries.meaning: Names the status, office, property, or established fact that entitles or enables the main event — the cause understood as a qualification rather than as a force.
examples: By virtue of her office, the vice president presides over the Senate.
He inherited the title by virtue of being the eldest son.
The clause is enforceable by virtue of Section 12 of the agreement.
By virtue of its size alone, the company sets the price for the whole region.
She had access to the files by virtue of her security clearance.
Sound travels faster through steel by virtue of its density.
entries.русский: в силу, на основании — книжн.; называет статус или качество, дающее право
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by virtue of being the oldest). Never a finite clause — for a clause you need by virtue of the fact that, which is heavy enough that because is almost always the better answer.
entries.pattern: [clause] by virtue of [noun phrase] · By virtue of [noun phrase], [clause] · by virtue of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: By virtue of names a qualification — a status, office, property, or fact that entitles or enables — where because of names a plain cause. He got in by virtue of his last name says the name functioned as a credential; he got in because of his last name says only that it was the reason. Against by dint of, which names effort rather than standing: by dint of hard work, but by virtue of seniority. Virtue here carries its old sense of "power, efficacy," not moral goodness.
entries.see also: by reason of, on the strength of, because of, by dint of, by virtue of (complex prepositions)

entries.meaning: The clipped, regional form of on account of. Recognize it, and write because of.
examples: "We never went, 'count of the creek was up."
School let out early 'count of the ice.
"It ain't 'count of the money," he said, "and you know it."
He quit the mill 'count of his back.
"On count of what happened last spring, nobody's asking her twice."
She stayed home 'count of being the only one in the house who could drive.
The verse is there 'count of the rhyme and nothing else.
entries.русский: из-за, потому как — простореч. и диал., стяжённое on account of
entries.register: nonstandard and regional — Southern, Appalachian, South Midland, and African American English speech. In print it is eye-dialect, and an American meets it in fiction, in song lyrics, and in oral-history transcripts, essentially never in edited prose.
entries.type: complex, aphetic — on account of with the front worn off
entries.variants: on count of keeps the on; 'count of and count of drop it; count o' drops the f as well. All of them are on account of at different stages of wear, and the apostrophe is the writer's mark rather than anything the speaker does.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund, exactly as with on account of — and, in the varieties where it lives, a full finite clause as well: 'count of it was raining. That clause is ordinary inside the dialect and nonstandard in edited writing, which is the same split the on account of entry describes. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] 'count of [noun phrase] · [clause] 'count of [verb-ing] · (dialect) [clause] 'count of [clause] · on count of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Not a separate preposition but a worn-down on account of, exactly as 'cause is a worn-down because — and the parallel runs all the way down, since both are unremarkable in speech, both are marked in writing, and both live mostly in reported dialogue. Use it to place a speaker in fiction; do not use it in your own prose, and do not treat the clause pattern as an error in somebody else's mouth. Against because of, the neutral written word, and against on account of, which is itself already one step down in register.
entries.see also: on account of, because of, along of, on account of (complex prepositions), 'cause (conjunction)

examples: Photograph courtesy of the National Archives.
Everyone got a ride home, courtesy of her uncle's van.
The map is reproduced courtesy of the state historical society.
The Rangers won it in overtime, courtesy of a deflection off a defenseman's skate.
Half of downtown was dry by noon, courtesy of a burst main on Sixth Street.
He spent the afternoon in the emergency room, courtesy of a ladder he should have thrown out years ago.
Video courtesy of KTLA; used with permission.
The lights came back on a little after four, courtesy of a crew that had been out since dawn.

senses.head: Supplied by; with the permission or generosity of
body: The literal credit line of captions and acknowledgments.

senses.head: Caused by, with a wry tip of the hat
body: The news and sports use, where the cause is as often unwelcome as welcome.
examples: Photograph courtesy of the National Archives.
Everyone got a ride home, courtesy of her uncle's van.
The map is reproduced courtesy of the state historical society.
The Rangers won it in overtime, courtesy of a deflection off a defenseman's skate.
Half of downtown was dry by noon, courtesy of a burst main on Sixth Street.
He spent the afternoon in the emergency room, courtesy of a ladder he should have thrown out years ago.
Video courtesy of KTLA; used with permission.
The lights came back on a little after four, courtesy of a crew that had been out since dawn.

entries.русский: любезно предоставлено кем-л.; тж. ирон. благодаря кому-л. — о неприятном
entries.register: neutral, and heavily journalistic — captions, credit lines, sportswriting
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, organization, or thing. No gerund, and never a finite clause. In photo credits it also appears bare, with the of dropped: photo courtesy the Newberry Library.
entries.pattern: [clause], courtesy of [noun phrase] · Courtesy of [noun phrase], [clause] · (credit line) Photograph courtesy of [name] · by courtesy of [noun phrase] (older, more formal)
entries.contrast: Thanks to with the credit spelled out. Both can be sincere or sarcastic, but courtesy of leans harder on agency — the thing named actually supplied the result — and it is far more common at the end of a sentence, tacked on as an afterthought, than at the front.
entries.see also: thanks to, because of, on account of, courtesy of (conjunctions catalog)

examples: The delay was due to fog over the bay.
Most of the increase is due to a change in how the data is collected.
Absences due to illness must be reported by nine.
Errors due to rounding may make the columns disagree.
Due to the holiday, there will be no pickup on Monday.
The clinic cut its hours due to being understaffed all summer.
Two flights were canceled due to mechanical problems.
The shortfall was due to a single contract nobody had budgeted for.
Service was suspended due to flooding on the lower platform.

senses.head: Attributable to; caused by — adjectival, after be or modifying a noun
body: The delay was due to fog.

senses.head: Because of — adverbial, modifying the whole clause. Standard in American English, still contested
body: Due to fog, the flight was canceled.
examples: The delay was due to fog over the bay.
Most of the increase is due to a change in how the data is collected.
Absences due to illness must be reported by nine.
Errors due to rounding may make the columns disagree.
Due to the holiday, there will be no pickup on Monday.
The clinic cut its hours due to being understaffed all summer.
Two flights were canceled due to mechanical problems.
The shortfall was due to a single contract nobody had budgeted for.
Service was suspended due to flooding on the lower platform.

entries.русский: вызванный чем-л., обусловленный чем-л.; наречно — из-за, по причине
entries.register: neutral, with a live usage dispute over sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (due to being understaffed). Never a finite clause — for a clause you need due to the fact that, which spends nine syllables on what because does in two. Note that be due to + a bare infinitive (the train is due to arrive at six) is a completely different construction: the adjective due plus a real infinitive, meaning "scheduled."
entries.pattern: [noun] is due to [noun phrase] · [noun] due to [noun phrase] · [clause] due to [noun phrase] · Due to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: See the due to vs. because of rule at the end of this file — this is the single most-taught prescriptive rule about causal prepositions and the one most widely ignored. In short: traditionalists allow due to only where attributable to would fit and where it attaches to a noun, and prescribe because of or owing to everywhere else. Because of is never wrong; due to sometimes is, depending entirely on your reader.
entries.see also: because of, owing to, on account of, as a result of, attributable to, due to (complex prepositions), due to the fact that (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Names an absence as the cause: the thing failed because something necessary was not there.
examples: The case was dismissed for lack of evidence.
The project died for lack of funding.
He agreed, for lack of a better option.
Call it a hunch, for lack of a better word.
Three houses burned for lack of a working hydrant.
She stayed in the job for lack of anywhere else to go.
entries.русский: за неимением, из-за нехватки чего-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a bare one with no article — for lack of evidence, for lack of funding, for lack of a better word. A gerund is possible but rare. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for lack of [noun phrase] · For lack of [noun phrase], [clause] · for lack of a better [noun] · for lack of anything better
entries.contrast: For lack of and for want of are one preposition in two vocabularies — lack is the everyday word, want the literary one — and for lack of is the one to use in ordinary American prose. Both name a missing cause: the reason something failed is that something else was absent. Watch the direction against because of: because of the evidence means the evidence caused it, for lack of evidence means the absence did.
entries.see also: for want of, because of, in the absence of, absent, but for

entries.meaning: The literary twin of for lack of: it names an absence as the cause of a failure, using want in its old sense of "shortage."
examples: For want of a nail the shoe was lost.
The bill failed for want of a second.
He called it a memoir, for want of a better term.
A dozen small farms went under for want of rain.
She read the manual twice for want of anything better to do.
The motion was denied for want of jurisdiction.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /fɚ ˈwɑnt ə/ · stressed for /fɔr/ · fer-WAHNT uhv
entries.русский: за неимением, за недостатком — книжн., с оттенком пословицы
entries.register: neutral to literary — proverbial, and noticeably formal in American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually bare (for want of a nail). A gerund is possible but unusual. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for want of [noun phrase] · For want of [noun phrase], [clause] · for want of a better [noun] · for want of anything better to do
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to for lack of; the whole difference is register. Want appears here in its old sense of "absence, shortage," which survives in modern American English almost nowhere else (wanting, in want of, for want of). Because that sense is opaque to most speakers, choosing for want of reads as a deliberate stylistic gesture rather than a neutral choice.
entries.see also: for lack of, because of, in the absence of, short of

entries.respell: weak /ɪn ˈlaɪt ə/, run together as /ɪn ˈlaɪtə/
entries.meaning: Names the new information or evidence in the light of which a decision is taken or reconsidered.
examples: In light of the new evidence, the district attorney reopened the case.
The board postponed the vote in light of the auditor's report.
In light of everything that's happened, a delay seems reasonable.
The policy was rewritten in light of last year's lawsuit.
In light of his record, the judge suspended the sentence.
We reconsidered in light of having lost two of our biggest accounts.
entries.русский: в свете чего-л., учитывая — о новых сведениях, а не о физической причине
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.variants: in the light of, with the article, is the dominant British form. American English strongly prefers in light of, and the article-less form is now spreading in British writing too.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in light of having missed two payments). Never a finite clause — use in light of the fact that if you must have one.
entries.pattern: In light of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in light of [noun phrase] · in light of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: In light of names the information that leads someone to a decision, not the physical force that produces an event. You cancel a launch in light of the forecast, but the rocket does not explode in light of a faulty valve — that is because of. Against in view of, the two are near-identical; in light of is commoner in American English and suggests something newly learned, while in view of suggests a standing circumstance.
entries.see also: in view of, on the grounds of, on the strength of, given, considering, in light of (complex prepositions)

entries.meaning: Names the statement or document somebody acted on, with the implication that acting on it was reasonable.
examples: She bought the lot in reliance on a survey the seller had commissioned.
The bank released the funds in reliance on the auditor's certificate.
In reliance on that promise, the tenant spent forty thousand dollars on the buildout.
The complaint alleges that he signed in reasonable reliance on projections the company knew were stale.
Investors purchased in reliance upon statements the company withdrew four months later.
Nothing at all was done in reliance on the email, which is exactly why the estoppel argument failed.
He turned down the other offer in reliance on being told the job was his.
entries.русский: полагаясь на, доверившись — юр.; о поступке, совершённом на основании заявления
entries.register: formal and legal — contracts, opinion letters, securities filings, and fraud and estoppel pleadings
entries.variants: in reliance upon is the heavier drafting form and is usual in older instruments. In reasonable reliance on and in justifiable reliance on are the pleading formulas, and the modifier there is doing legal work rather than decorating.
entries.complement: noun phrase — a statement, representation, promise, opinion, certificate, or document — or a gerund (in reliance on being told the title was clear). Never a finite clause. The clause hangs off the noun instead: in in reliance on the representation that the title was clear, the that belongs to representation, not to the preposition.
entries.pattern: [clause] in reliance on [noun phrase] · In reliance on [noun phrase], [clause] · in reasonable reliance on [noun phrase] · in reliance upon [noun phrase] · in reliance on [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Names the statement somebody acted on, and the acting is the point — reliance with no act behind it carries no legal weight, which is why the phrase attaches to verbs of doing: signed, paid, bought, forbore, spent. Against on the strength of, the everyday equivalent, which names a demonstration that persuaded; in reliance on names something asserted and adds the claim that the actor was entitled to believe it. Against in light of, which names information a decision took account of and says nothing about who supplied it or whether it was true. Against on the basis of, which is colder and merely procedural.
entries.see also: on the strength of, in light of, by virtue of, on the basis of, dependence on/reliance on

entries.meaning: Names the standing circumstance that a decision takes account of — the formal way of saying given.
examples: In view of his age, the court imposed probation instead.
The fee was waived in view of the delay on our end.
In view of the weather, the ceremony has been moved indoors.
The trial was halted early in view of the risks involved.
No further action was taken in view of the company's cooperation.
In view of having already paid twice, she refused the third invoice.
entries.русский: ввиду, принимая во внимание — книжн.; об уже имеющемся обстоятельстве
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a finite clause — in view of the fact that for a clause.
entries.pattern: In view of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in view of [noun phrase] · in view of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The literal spatial phrase in view of — "within sight of," as in a cabin in view of the lake — is a different animal and is not a preposition of cause; only the abstract use belongs here, and context always separates them. Against in light of: both name grounds for a decision, but in view of points at a circumstance already in place (in view of his age) where in light of points at something newly learned (in light of the report). Both are more formal than given and much more formal than since.
entries.see also: in light of, on the grounds of, given, considering, in view of (complex prepositions)

entries.meaning: Names a cause in the plainest available words, with a spoken flavor that because of does not have.
examples: School was closed on account of the ice.
On account of the recall, we're two weeks behind.
He couldn't travel on account of his knee.
She got the extension on account of being in the hospital.
The store closed early on account of the power outage.
On account of the drought, the town banned outdoor watering.
entries.русский: из-за, по причине — нейтр. на письме, разг. в речи
entries.register: neutral in writing, colloquial in speech — and the clause use is nonstandard
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on account of being sick). In standard written English, never a finite clause — but on account of he was sick, with a full clause, is a real and widespread spoken form in Southern, Midland, and African American English, and the folk-doubled on account of because belongs to the same register. Recognize both; do not write either in edited prose.
entries.pattern: [clause] on account of [noun phrase] · On account of [noun phrase], [clause] · on account of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: A plain synonym of because of — one register down in speech, one register up in older writing. Do not confuse the causal preposition with the accounting phrase on account ("as partial payment") or with on someone's account ("for someone's sake"): don't stay on my account means "not for my sake," not "not because of me."
entries.see also: because of, due to, owing to, thanks to, on account of (complex prepositions), on account of the fact that (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Names the stated justification for a decision, a refusal, a claim, or a legal action.
examples: The claim was denied on the grounds of a pre-existing condition.
Discrimination on the grounds of age is prohibited.
He refused to testify on the grounds of self-incrimination.
The documents were withheld on grounds of national security.
She filed on the grounds of desertion.
The appeal was rejected on the grounds of untimeliness.
entries.русский: на основании, по причине — офиц. и юр.; о заявленном основании
entries.register: formal and legal
entries.variants: on grounds of, without the article, is standard in journalism and legal drafting. The singular on the ground of is older and now mainly British.
entries.never a finite clause: the clause form is on the grounds that, which is a conjunction, not this preposition.
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically an abstract noun naming a category of justification (race, cruelty, national security, self-incrimination). A gerund is possible but stiff.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the grounds of [noun phrase] · [clause] on grounds of [noun phrase] · on the grounds that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: On the grounds of + noun phrase, on the grounds that + clause is the pair to memorize; splicing them (on the grounds of he lied) is the standard error. Against because of, this phrase names a justification somebody offered, not a cause operating in the world: a permit is denied on the grounds of zoning, but a roof does not collapse on the grounds of snow. Against on the basis of, which points at evidence rather than at a reason for a decision. Against on the pretext of, which is the same phrase with the writer's judgment added: on the grounds of leaves open whether the stated reason is the true one, on the pretext of says it is not.
entries.see also: on the pretext of, by reason of, in view of, on the strength of, on the basis of, on the grounds that (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Names the false reason somebody gave — the excuse offered to cover the real motive.
examples: He got into the building on the pretext of delivering a package.
The troops crossed the border under the pretext of a training exercise.
She left the table on the pretext of a call she had to take.
Editors killed the piece on the pretext of space, and everybody knew better.
Under the pretext of reviewing the budget, the committee reopened the whole contract.
He came by twice a week on the pretext of returning tools he had never borrowed.
The stop was made on the pretext of a broken taillight.
entries.русский: под предлогом — утверждает, что названная причина ложная
entries.register: neutral to formal — journalism, history, and narrative
entries.variants: under the pretext of is at least as common in American English and is a shade more accusatory. On the pretense of is a near-synonym; under the guise of stresses the disguise rather than the excuse, and takes a noun more readily than a gerund.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on the pretext of checking the meter). Never a finite clause — the clause form is on the pretext that + clause, which is a conjunction: on the pretext that the meter needed checking.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the pretext of [verb-ing] · [clause] under the pretext of [noun phrase] · on the pretext that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: The dishonest twin of on the grounds of. Both name a stated reason rather than an operating cause, but on the grounds of is neutral about whether the stated reason is the real one, while on the pretext of asserts that it is not: a permit denied on the grounds of zoning may well be about zoning, but a search conducted on the pretext of a broken taillight is not about the taillight. Because the phrase commits the writer to that judgment, you cannot use it of your own motives except as a joke. Against in the name of, which names a value invoked as cover and leaves the sincerity open.
entries.see also: on the grounds of, in the name of, because of, for the purpose of, on the grounds that (conjunction)

entries.meaning: Names the demonstration, showing, or asset that persuaded someone to act.
examples: She was hired on the strength of one interview.
The bank lent them the money on the strength of a signed letter of intent.
On the strength of two good quarters, the board approved the expansion.
He got the part on the strength of a two-minute audition tape.
The town issued bonds on the strength of projected tourism revenue.
They took the deal on the strength of having worked with the buyer before.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ən ðə ˈstrɛŋkθ ə/ · on-thuh-STRENGKTH uhv
entries.русский: полагаясь на, основываясь на — о том, что убедило человека действовать
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on the strength of having worked with them before). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the strength of [noun phrase] · On the strength of [noun phrase], [clause] · on the strength of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Names the evidence or asset somebody relied on when they acted — a recommendation, a demo, one good quarter. Because of would state the cause flatly; on the strength of says the actor weighed something and found it convincing, and it carries a faint hint that the weighing may yet prove to have been optimistic. Against by virtue of, which names a standing status rather than a demonstration, and against on the basis of, which is colder and more procedural.
entries.see also: by virtue of, on the grounds of, in light of, on the basis of

examples: I asked out of curiosity, not because I doubted her.
He kept the letters out of sentiment.
They took the dog in out of pity.
She resigned out of loyalty to her staff, not out of anger.
Most of them show up out of habit.
He agreed out of sheer exhaustion.
The company recalled the batch out of an abundance of caution.
The whole program grew out of one complaint letter.
Nothing useful came out of the second meeting.
Two good ideas came out of an afternoon nobody had wanted to sit through.
Out of options and nearly out of time, they settled on the courthouse steps.
Out of patience with a third round of revisions, she pulled the piece.

senses.head: The motive inside the actor
body: The feeling, disposition, or state of mind an action springs from, named by a bare abstract noun. I asked out of curiosity.

senses.head: The source something developed from
body: With verbs of emergence — come, grow, arise, develop — naming the episode a later thing grew out of. The whole program grew out of one complaint letter.

senses.head: The resource run down to nothing, offered as a reason
body: Almost always fronted and absolute, naming the shortage that forced the outcome. Out of options, they settled.
examples: I asked out of curiosity, not because I doubted her.
He kept the letters out of sentiment.
They took the dog in out of pity.
She resigned out of loyalty to her staff, not out of anger.
Most of them show up out of habit.
He agreed out of sheer exhaustion.
The company recalled the batch out of an abundance of caution.
The whole program grew out of one complaint letter.
Nothing useful came out of the second meeting.
Two good ideas came out of an afternoon nobody had wanted to sit through.
Out of options and nearly out of time, they settled on the courthouse steps.
Out of patience with a third round of revisions, she pulled the piece.

entries.русский: из, по — о побуждении: из любопытства, из страха; тж. из-за нехватки чего-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: in the motive sense (1), a bare abstract noun with no determiner — out of curiosity, out of spite, out of respect, out of habit. An article usually breaks it: out of a sense of duty works only because the head noun is sense, while out of the curiosity is impossible. A gerund is marginal in this sense (out of not wanting to embarrass her occurs and grates). In the source sense (2) the complement is an ordinary noun phrase with its determiners intact — out of that meeting, out of one complaint letter — and a fused relative works there as well, which is still a noun phrase and not a clause: something good came out of what happened. In the exhaustion sense (3) it is again a bare noun, this time naming a resource: out of options, out of time, out of patience. ✗ Never a that-clause in any sense, and no other finite clause either. ✗ Bare out is a different word: it is an adverb or a verb particle and takes no object at all (she walked out, cross it out, the truth came out), where out of is the two-word preposition and always requires one — the truth came out against the truth came out of a deposition nobody read. (The spatial out of — out of the house — is treated with the prepositions of movement, and the full six-sense account of the word, proportions and made out of included, is at out of.)
entries.pattern: [clause] out of [bare abstract noun] · Out of [bare abstract noun], [clause] · out of a sense of [noun] · out of respect / fear / spite / habit / necessity / curiosity / desperation · [come / grow / arise / develop] out of [noun phrase] · Out of [resource noun], [clause]
entries.contrast: In sense 1 out of names the motive inside the actor — the feeling or disposition the action came out of — where because of names a cause outside. She lied out of fear is about her state; she lied because of the threat is about the threat. The determinerless noun is the surest sign you are in this sense rather than the spatial one. Against from, which overlaps in acted from a sense of duty but sounds more literary; see from. Sense 2 is the ancestor of the legal arising out of, and there the direction reverses: the object is the origin and the subject is what grew from it. Sense 3 is the mirror of for lack of — both make an absence the reason — but for lack of names what was never there and out of names what ran out.
entries.see also: through, for fear of, because of, arising from, from, out of (movement), out of (complex prepositions)

examples: The strike began as an argument over scheduling software.
Two counties have been in court over the same forty acres since 2003.
Congress deadlocked over the disaster funding bill.
There is still disagreement over whether the vote was binding.
Nobody could explain the confusion over how the money had been spent.
The deputy director resigned over the handling of the complaint.
The city was sued over the condition of the pumping station.
Two officers were suspended over failing to report the incident.
He's still beating himself up over one bad quarter.
She lost a week's sleep over a two-line email.
There's no use crying over spilled milk.
The whole family fussed over the baby for an hour.
Critics raved over a record the band itself had written off.

senses.head: The point of contention — what two parties are in conflict about
body: A ten-year fight over water rights.

senses.head: The trigger of a strong reaction — a resignation, a lawsuit, an arrest, a firing
body: He resigned over the handling of the complaint.

senses.head: The object of grief, worry, or regret — what somebody frets or mourns about
body: There's no use crying over spilled milk.

senses.head: The object of a fuss — what somebody makes too much of, admiring as readily as complaining
body: They fussed over the baby all afternoon.
examples: The strike began as an argument over scheduling software.
