entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪn ðə ˈɪntrəst ə/ · in-thee-IN-truhst uhv
entries.русский: в интересах, ради — ради экономии времени; тж. в интересах кого-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal — the institutional word
entries.variants: in the interests of, plural, is fully standard and is the dominant form in British English. American English uses both, with the singular slightly ahead in edited prose; in the interest of time is fixed in the singular.
entries.complement: noun phrase — most often an abstract noun naming a value (time, fairness, safety, transparency, full disclosure) — or a party whose interests are being served, or a gerund, which is fully idiomatic here: in the interest of avoiding delay, in the interest of getting this done today. Never a bare infinitive (in the interest of to avoid delay) and never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: In the interest of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in the interest of [noun phrase] · in the interests of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Overlaps for the sake of in the abstract sense — in the interest of clarity and for the sake of clarity are interchangeable — and differs only in tone: in the interest of belongs to meetings, memos, and disclosures, where for the sake of is personal. With a party rather than a value it means "to that party's advantage" and shades toward for the benefit of.
entries.see also: for the sake of, for the benefit of, on behalf of, in the interest of (conjunctions catalog)

entries.meaning: Names the thing an act is meant to stand for: the gesture is a sign rather than a means.
examples: He handed over his sword in token of surrender.
The rings were exchanged in token of a promise neither of them could yet keep.
In token of good faith, the buyer wired half the deposit that afternoon.
Belts of wampum were sent in token of peace.
In token whereof the parties have set their hands this tenth day of June.
She kept the pressed flower in token of an afternoon nobody else remembered.
The delegation bowed in token of submission and meant not a word of it.
entries.русский: в знак чего-л. — устар. и торж.; поступок как символ, а не как средство
entries.register: archaic and ceremonial — the King James Bible, nineteenth-century prose, treaty and deed language, and set-piece presentation speeches. In ordinary modern American English it is dead, and using it is a deliberately antique gesture.
entries.variants: as a token of is the living modern form and is what to write — as a token of our appreciation. In token whereof is the deed-and-treaty formula and a close cousin of in witness whereof.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming what is being signified — esteem, good faith, submission, friendship, our appreciation, peace. No gerund (✗ in token of thanking them) and never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in token of [noun phrase] · In token of [noun phrase], [clause] · in token whereof (the formula) · as a token of [noun phrase] (the modern form)
entries.contrast: The object is not a purpose but a meaning: the act is done to stand for something, not to accomplish it. That is what separates it from for the purpose of and from in recognition of — a ring given in token of a promise is that promise made visible, where a medal given in recognition of service only acknowledges the service. Modern American English does the same work with as a token of or as a sign of. Nothing to do with the ordinary modern senses of token — a subway token, a token gesture, a security token — though every one of them descends from this one.
entries.see also: in recognition of, in honor of, in witness whereof, in consideration of, by way of

entries.meaning: Names the penalty that will follow if an obligation is not met — purpose expressed as a threat.
examples: Witnesses were ordered to appear on pain of contempt.
The edict forbade the assembly on pain of death.
Employees must report the conflict under pain of dismissal.
The rule required silence at table on pain of penance.
On pain of being held in contempt, he finally produced the calendar.
Deadlines here are real: file by the fifth, under pain of a late fee that doubles every week.
The license bars re-export on pain of losing it altogether.
entries.русский: под страхом (наказания) — юр. и книжн.; «под страхом смерти»
entries.register: formal and legal with a literary streak — court orders, older statutes, church and military discipline, and rhetoric. In ordinary American speech it is a deliberate flourish, and an American most often meets it in the fixed on pain of death.
entries.variants: under pain of is at least as common in American English and is the dominant form with death; upon pain of is the archaic third. All three are one phrase and none is more correct than the others. The related under penalty of — as in under penalty of perjury — is a separate fixed formula and is not a variant of this one.
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a penalty — death, dismissal, contempt, excommunication, a fine, forfeiture — or a gerund naming that penalty as an event: on pain of being held in contempt, under pain of being fined. Never a bare infinitive (✗ on pain of to be fined) and never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [command or obligation], on pain of [penalty] · under pain of [penalty] · on pain of death · on pain of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Purpose stated as a threat. The phrase names not the aim of the act but the penalty for failing to perform it, which makes it the mirror of for fear of: for fear of looks out from inside the actor and names what they are avoiding, while on pain of is imposed from outside and names what will be done to them. It attaches to an obligation and never to a completed act — he was ordered to appear on pain of arrest works, ✗ he appeared on pain of arrest does not, because the penalty is conditional on failure and failure did not happen. Against under penalty of, the American oath formula, which certifies that something is true rather than threatening someone who does not act.
entries.see also: for fear of, in obedience to, in mitigation of, by reason of, pursuant to

entries.meaning: States purpose with an infinitive, in a register a step above in order to, and is at its most idiomatic in the negative so as not to. Like in order to it can never take a noun.
examples: He spoke quietly so as not to wake the baby.
Fold the corner so as to leave a half-inch margin.
They staggered the shifts so as to keep the line running.
She phrased it carefully so as not to commit to anything.
The panels are angled so as to catch the afternoon sun.
Pack the mugs in newspaper so as not to chip them.
entries.русский: чтобы, так чтобы — книжн., чаще на письме, чем в речи
entries.register: formal — commoner in writing than in speech
entries.complement: a bare infinitive verb, and nothing else — like in order to and unlike everything else in this section. So as to avoid delay, never so as to avoidance, never so as to avoiding. The negative so as not to is extremely common and is in fact the phrase's most frequent use. The understood subject of the infinitive must match the subject of the main clause; if it does not, the sentence dangles — So as to save time, the meeting was shortened leaves nobody saving time.
entries.pattern: [clause] so as to [verb] · [clause] so as not to [verb]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in order to in meaning, with two differences that matter. First, so as to is more formal and much rarer in speech. Second, it resists fronting: In order to save time, we skipped lunch is natural, So as to save time, we skipped lunch is stilted. It is at its most idiomatic in the negative, where so as not to wake her beats in order not to wake her every time. Keep it separate from the result correlative so … as to (so cold as to be dangerous), which is a different construction with a word wedged in the middle.
entries.see also: in order to, in an effort to, for the purpose of, to, so as to (conjunctions catalog), so that (conjunction)

entries.meaning: States a purpose or eventual intention behind an action, in formal register. Its to is a preposition, so the verb after it must be a gerund.
examples: The two sides met with a view to resolving the dispute before trial.
The land was bought with a view to eventual development.
Records are retained with a view to possible litigation.
She took the assistant's job with a view to learning the business.
With a view to cutting overhead, the firm subleased two floors.
The treaty was drafted with a view to the accession of new members.
entries.русский: с целью, с прицелом на — книжн.; требует герундия, а не инфинитива
entries.register: formal — business, diplomatic, and legal writing
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive. With a view to reducing costs is correct; with a view to reduce costs is an error, and a very common one, because the to looks like an infinitive marker and is not. It is a preposition, and prepositions take -ing. The test is substitution: if with a view to reduction works, the slot belongs to a preposition and the verb must be -ing. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with a view to [verb-ing] · [clause] with a view to [noun phrase] · With a view to [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: The classic to-plus-gerund trap, in the same family as look forward to, be committed to, object to, and be used to. Against in order to, which takes the infinitive this phrase forbids — identical meaning, opposite grammar. Against with an eye to and with the aim of, which take the same gerund and sound less formal. With a view of is a different phrase entirely and means "with a sight of": a room with a view of the harbor. Note that this is the one purpose phrase the of-test does not sort: it ends in to and still takes a gerund, which is why it has to be learned as an exception — compare with intent to defraud, where the to really is an infinitive marker.
entries.see also: with an eye to, with the aim of, in order to, for the purpose of, with a view to (complex prepositions)

entries.meaning: States a purpose held in mind while something else is being done — the plain American equivalent of with a view to.
examples: They renovated the top floor with an eye to renting it out.
The city rezoned the district with an eye toward attracting light manufacturing.
She's taking statistics with an eye to graduate school.
The contract was written with an eye to the next negotiation.
With an eye toward the fall election, the governor delayed the announcement.
He buys used equipment with an eye to reselling it in the spring.
entries.русский: с расчётом на, имея в виду — проще и живее, чем with a view to
entries.register: neutral — plainer than with a view to, and common in journalism
entries.variants: with an eye toward and with an eye towards are both current; American English prefers toward, and uses with an eye toward at least as often as the bare to form. With an eye on is a different phrase and means "watching."
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive, exactly as with with a view to. With an eye to expanding, not with an eye to expand. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with an eye to [verb-ing] · [clause] with an eye toward [noun phrase] · With an eye to [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: The everyday American equivalent of with a view to, and the one to reach for if you want the idea without the boardroom register. It adds a note of watchfulness — the purpose is being held in mind while something else is done — which is why it takes so naturally to toward. Keep it apart from with an eye on, which means monitoring rather than aiming: with an eye on the clock watches the clock, while with an eye to the clock would make the clock the goal.
entries.see also: with a view to, with intent to, with the aim of, in order to, toward

entries.meaning: States a purpose as an element of an offense or a legal act, in the infinitive frame American criminal statutes use.
examples: He was charged with possession with intent to distribute.
The statute reaches any false statement made with intent to deceive a federal agency.
Breaking and entering with intent to commit a felony carries the longer sentence.
She signed the transfer with intent to put the assets beyond her creditors' reach.
The complaint alleges he altered the log with the intent to mislead the auditors.
The forms were backdated with intent to claim a credit the company had already lost.
Loitering with intent to solicit was struck down as unconstitutionally vague.
entries.русский: с намерением, с умыслом — юр., формула умысла в уголовных статьях
entries.register: legal — the standard mens rea formula of American criminal statutes and charging documents
entries.variants: with the intent to takes the same infinitive and is the fuller statutory form. Do not treat with the intention of as a variant: it takes a gerund — with the intention of defrauding, never with the intention of to defraud and never with the intention to defraud in careful prose; see with the aim of.
entries.complement: a bare infinitive verb. With intent to defraud, with intent to distribute, with intent to deprive — never with intent to defrauding and never with intent of defrauding. It is the only with-purpose phrase on the infinitive side of the split, and it is there because there is no of in it. Never a finite clause — the clause form is with the intent that + clause.
entries.pattern: [verb] with intent to [verb] · with the intent to [verb] · possession with intent to distribute · with the intent that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.the most useful minimal pair in this sec: with intent to defraud (infinitive, no of) against with the intention of defrauding (gerund, with of). Same meaning, opposite grammar, and the of is the tell. The rule holds across the whole section — of takes the gerund, bare to takes the infinitive — with with a view to as the lone exception, since its to is a preposition. Against with the aim of, which is the everyday phrase: with intent to belongs where the purpose is an element somebody has to prove.
entries.see also: with the aim of, with a view to, in order to, so as to, for the purpose of, with the intent that (conjunction)

entries.meaning: States the goal an action is designed to reach, in plain neutral register, with a gerund after of. ---
examples: The program was set up with the aim of cutting emergency-room visits.
He wrote the memo with the aim of getting the decision on the record.
With the aim of speeding up review, the agency added two examiners.
They merged the two departments with the aim of eliminating duplicate work.
The study was designed with the aim of settling the question for good.
She entered the country with the intention of staying permanently.
entries.русский: с целью — книжн., просто называет цель; с герундием
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.variants: with the intention of, with the goal of, and with the object of are built identically, take the same gerund, and differ only in weight; with the intention of stresses that the purpose was deliberate, which does real work in legal contexts where intent is an element of the offense.
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive. With the aim of reducing waste, not with the aim of to reduce waste and not with the aim to reduce waste. (With the aim to does occur and is widely judged an error.) Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with the aim of [verb-ing] · [clause] with the aim of [noun phrase] · With the aim of [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: The plainest of the with-purpose phrases: with a view to is more formal, with an eye to more watchful, and with the aim of simply states the target. Where with the intention of replaces it, the emphasis shifts from the target to the actor's state of mind, which is exactly why criminal pleadings prefer intent. Note that they prefer it in the infinitive frame with intent to, not in this one: with intent to defraud against with the intention of defrauding, and never with the intention to defraud.
entries.see also: with a view to, with an eye to, in the hope of, for the purpose of, in order to, with the aim of (conjunctions catalog)
